title: Riteish Deshmukh Spent Ten Years Becoming a King. This Friday, 'Raja Shivaji' Storms Netflix Worldwide.
excerpt: The Marathi epic that became only the second film in its language to cross ₹100 crore lands on Netflix on June 26 — and yes, Salman Khan's sword-swinging cameo travels with it.
body:
It opens the way the best historical epics do: not with a battle, but with a boy. A child in Jijabai's courtyard, learning that a kingdom is something you build rather than inherit. By the time **Riteish Deshmukh** fills the frame as a grown Chhatrapati Shivaji Maharaj — beard streaked, eyes steady, the weight of a whole people on his shoulders — you understand why this man spent ten years chasing the role. *Raja Shivaji* was never a film for him. It was a vow.

<youtube>https://youtube.com/watch?v=Bgy00eaFyhE</youtube>

https://x.com/NetflixIndia/status/2070009089904570542

And this Friday, June 26, that vow goes global. Netflix has locked the streaming rights to the Marathi blockbuster, dropping it in Marathi, Hindi and Telugu — which means the NRI uncle in New Jersey who's been waiting two months to see what the fuss was about finally gets his weekend plan.



> **"It opened to a record-shattering ₹40.35 crore first weekend, the biggest ever for a Marathi film, then refused to slow down."**


The fuss, for the record, was considerable. *Raja Shivaji* didn't just open well when it hit theatres on May 1 — Maharashtra Day, naturally, because subtlety has never been this film's brand. It opened to a record-shattering ₹40.35 crore first weekend, the biggest ever for a Marathi film, then refused to slow down. It crossed ₹100 crore gross, becoming only the **second Marathi film in history** to do it, trailing only the immortal *Sairat*. Trade pundits now peg the lifetime finish past ₹125 crore. For an industry long treated as Bollywood's quieter cousin, those are statement numbers.


![Chhatrapati Shivaji Maharaj — Photo: Wikimedia Commons](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/e/ea/Shivaji_British_Museum.jpg)


> "Riteish didn't play Shivaji. For three hours, he disappeared into him." — a line that ran across half of Marathi Twitter on opening weekend

Let's talk about the ensemble, because this is where the film flexes. **Sanjay Dutt** is the antagonist Afzal Khan, and he plays menace the way only Dutt can — slow, amused, lethal. **Vidya Balan** turns up in a regal turn as Badi Sahiba. **Abhishek Bachchan**, **Bhagyashree**, **Fardeen Khan** and **Genelia Deshmukh** round out a cast that spans industries and decades. And in a casting decision that broke the internet before a single ticket was sold, **Salman Khan** appears as Jeeva Mahala — the loyal warrior who, in history and on screen, throws himself between Shivaji and an assassin's blade. Khan's cameo is brief, brutal and built around close-up action choreography sharp enough to draw applause in single-screens across Maharashtra. He filmed it over four days last November, and it shows: he's not phoning it in.

There's a sweet footnote too. Riteish's son **Rahyl Deshmukh** makes his acting debut as the young Shivaji — a father directing his boy in the story of a king who was, above all, his mother's son. The film knows exactly how much that mirror is worth.

Visually, *Raja Shivaji* is built for the small screen to strain against. Director Riteish Deshmukh — yes, he directed it too, his most audacious bet yet — shoots the Maratha hill forts like cathedrals, all stone and sky and torchlight. The CBFC, in clearing the three-hour-plus cut, asked for date slates and historical disclaimers; what they couldn't touch was the scale. This is a film that wants to be seen big, and on a half-decent diaspora living-room setup, it'll get close.

The timing is shrewd. *Raja Shivaji* lands the same Friday **Welcome To The Jungle** packs theatres, giving Indian audiences abroad a genuine choice: laugh in a cinema, or settle in at home with a warrior king. For the diaspora — especially the Maharashtrian families in the Bay Area, London and Toronto who've been swapping pirated-clip warnings for weeks — there's no contest. This is comfort cinema with a spine, the kind of film you put on for visiting parents and end up watching twice.

What *Raja Shivaji* really proves is harder to put in a box-office column. It's that a regional epic, made with conviction and a refusal to dumb itself down, can travel — across languages, across oceans, onto the same platform that beams *Stranger Things* into the same homes. Riteish Deshmukh spent a decade becoming a king. Starting Friday, the whole world gets to bow.

*Raja Shivaji streams on Netflix from June 26, 2026, in Marathi, Hindi and Telugu — available worldwide, including the US, UK and Canada.*
